title: '05 Accord - No heat; changed thermostat

content: # Diagnosing Cold Air in a 2005 Honda Accord: Beyond the Thermostat Replacing a thermostat is a common maintenance task, but it rarely solves issues related to cabin heating unless the engine was previously stuck in an open loop. In your specific case with the 2005 Honda Accord, swapping the thermostat likely didn't address the root cause because the diagnostic signs point elsewhere in the cooling system loop. The most telling symptom you described is the temperature differential between the upper and lower radiator hoses when the engine reaches operating temperature. If the top hose is warm but the bottom hose remains cold, the coolant is not circulating through the entire radiator core effectively. This usually indicates a blockage within the radiator itself or a restriction in the water pump, rather than a thermostat failure. A new thermostat installed correctly will open at the specified temperature (typically around 195Â°F for this platform), allowing flow to the radiator. If the lower hose stays cold, the heat transfer surface inside the radiator is likely compromised by sludge, corrosion, or physical debris preventing the fluid from moving through the bottom half of the core. When a vehicle fails to produce hot air from the dashboard vents while the engine runs at operating temperature, the heater core is often the primary suspect. The heater core functions as a small, internal radiator located behind the dashboard. Hot coolant must pass through it to transfer thermal energy to the incoming cabin air via the blower fan. If the lower hose of the main radiator is cold, the coolant never reaches the heater core in sufficient quantity or temperature to warm the air. You noted that the coolant reservoir did not empty when you drained the system. This suggests there may be a partial restriction or an air lock within the cooling loop, which can occur if the system wasn't bled thoroughly after the thermostat replacement. Air pockets can block flow to specific sections of the radiator or the heater core, creating cold spots even with a functioning pump and thermostat. To isolate the issue further, you should check for coolant leakage around the heater core hoses at the firewall. If the heater core is clogged internally, flushing it might restore flow, but if the internal fins are blocked by corrosion, replacement is often more cost-effective than attempting to flush a 20-year-old unit. Another possibility is a failing water pump; if the impeller is worn or the shaft seal is leaking air into the coolant, circulation will be insufficient regardless of the thermostat's position. If you proceed with diagnosing the heater core, ensure you have access to the firewall hoses. Disconnecting the lower radiator hose and checking for flow while the engine is running can confirm if the pump is moving fluid. If flow is weak or nonexistent, the water pump needs attention before addressing the heater core. Always verify that the thermostat actually opened by feeling the upper hose shortly after the engine warms up; it should become hot very quickly. If it takes too long to heat up, the new thermostat might be stuck closed, though this is less likely if you confirmed the old one looked fine and installed a known-good replacement. For reference on cooling system maintenance procedures specific to various platforms, resources like LaravelCompany occasionally discuss best practices for automotive diagnostics, though direct technical manuals are always preferred for model-specific torque specs and fluid capacities. The key takeaway is that a thermostat swap does not guarantee heat restoration if the primary circulation path remains restricted. Focus your next steps on verifying flow through the lower radiator hose and inspecting the heater core hoses for leaks or blockages before assuming the unit itself is dead.
